::: {.callout-note title="Before you start"}
Read [Diblock copolymer](diblock-copolymer.qmd) and
[What is a reference point?](reference-points.qmd). This page keeps the
construction explicit: one `Add`, then individual `Link` calls.
:::

**A complete structure can be used as a subunit in a larger structure.**
Build an arm from a thin rod and a solid cylinder, then attach nine copies
at a common junction. The rod and cylinder remain inside every copy.

All components live in the same `World`. Lengths are in nm and q in nm⁻¹.

## 1. Build one arm from a rod and a cylinder

The rod's second endpoint connects to the centre of the cylinder's bottom
face. Its first endpoint remains available for attaching the arm:

```text
rod.end1 -------- rod.end2 = cylinder.bottom [ cylinder ] cylinder.top
```

```{python}
import pyseb

world = pyseb.World("RodCylinderStar")
arm = world.Add("ThinRod", "rod")
world.Link("SolidCylinder", "cylinder.bottom", "rod.end2")
world.Add(arm, "arm")

parameters = {
    "L_rod": 12.0,
    "beta_rod": 1.0,
    "R_cylinder": 1.2,
    "L_cylinder": 6.0,
    "beta_cylinder": 1.0,
}

view_options = pyseb.USDExportOptions(pyseb.LengthUnit.Nanometer)
view_options.seed = 7
view_options.layout_mode = pyseb.LayoutMode.Readable

arm_view = pyseb.visualize(world, "arm", parameters, view_options, height=400)
```

The view shows two different subunits: a thin line for the rod and a solid
cylinder. Both are rigid internally, but their junction is freely jointed.
Their relative orientation in the view is one realization of the model.

`arm` is the graph describing this connected pair. We can now use that graph
as a building block, keeping its internal link intact.

## 2. Use the arm as a subunit to build a star

Previously, the first argument to `Add` or `Link` was a type such as
`"ThinRod"`. Now pass **`arm`**, the structure we just built:

```{python}
star = world.Add(arm, "arm1")
world.Link(arm, "arm2:rod.end1", "arm1:rod.end1")
world.Link(arm, "arm3:rod.end1", "arm1:rod.end1")
world.Link(arm, "arm4:rod.end1", "arm1:rod.end1")
world.Link(arm, "arm5:rod.end1", "arm1:rod.end1")
world.Link(arm, "arm6:rod.end1", "arm1:rod.end1")
world.Link(arm, "arm7:rod.end1", "arm1:rod.end1")
world.Link(arm, "arm8:rod.end1", "arm1:rod.end1")
world.Link(arm, "arm9:rod.end1", "arm1:rod.end1")
world.Add(star, "star")

star_view = pyseb.visualize(world, "star", parameters, view_options, height=560)
```

Each `Link` adds a **complete arm**, containing its rod, cylinder, and their
connection. There are now nine rods and nine cylinders. We wrote the
internal rod–cylinder link only once.

All nine `rod.end1` references meet at the same central junction. The junction
itself adds no scattering material. The arms can rotate freely; this is a
star topology, not a rigid object with fixed angles between its spokes.

## 3. Read a reference inside a structure

The colon in `arm2:rod.end1` means “inside arm2”:

| Part of the path | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `arm2` | Which instance of the complete arm |
| `rod` | Which subunit inside that instance |
| `end1` | Which reference on that subunit |

So `arm2:rod.end1` and `arm1:rod.end1` address different rods. The `Link` call
joins those particular reference locations.

The copies retain the internal parameter names. `L_rod` therefore controls
the rod length in **all nine arms**, and `R_cylinder` controls all nine
cylinder radii. The same parameter dictionary works for the single arm and
the complete star.

## 4. Calculate the scattering of each structure

The star can be evaluated as one structure even though it contains eighteen
primitive subunits:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

q = np.geomspace(0.001, 2.0, 180)
arm_curve = world.EvaluateFormFactor("arm", parameters, q.tolist())
star_curve = world.EvaluateFormFactor("star", parameters, q.tolist())

plt.loglog(q, arm_curve, label="One rod–cylinder arm")
plt.loglog(q, star_curve, label="Star of nine identical arms")
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ [nm$^{-1}$]")
plt.ylabel("Normalized form factor F(q)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

These are normalized curves: both start at one, despite their different total
scattering lengths. The star calculation includes scattering from every arm
and interference between arms. Its internal rods and cylinders have not
been replaced by a different particle model.

The viewers use seeded, readability-optimized orientations to make the arms
easier to distinguish. Scattering averages over the
orientations allowed by the freely jointed links; displayed overlaps do not
introduce excluded-volume interactions.
